newsitem.title: GHANA: Report points finger at two Ghana ministers.
newsitem.headline: Report points finger at two Ghana ministers.

text.p: Ghana's Commission of Human Rights and Justice accused two government ministers of actual or suspected irregularities on Thursday, in a report designed to clear the air before December's national elections.

The report, commissioned after reports in pro-opposition newspapers alleged corruption involving leading members of the administration, singled out Trade and Industry Minister Ibrahim Adam and Interior Minister Colonel Osei Owusu for criticism.

It said sacked presidential advisor for cocoa affairs Isaac Adjei-Maafo should be "severely reprimanded" for conduct incompatible with high office but cleared powerful Presidential Advisor on Governmental Affairs Paul-Victor Obeng of any wrong doing.

"The Commission finds that none of the numerous allegations levelled against the Presidential Advisor could be substantiated," the report said. Obeng "has neither acquired wealth illegally, nor is there any support of the allegations of corruption made against him."

President Jerry Rawlings, who seeks a final term in the December 7 presidential election, appointed the three Commission members under the terms of the constitution but has no power to dismiss them. All three are judges.
The report, published on Thursday, said Adam's ministry, while he was food and agriculture minister, gave undeserved waivers of customs duties and other taxes to fishing companies.
"(This) has occasioned loss of billions of cedis in revenue to the state," according to the report.
It said there was no immediate evidence the minister, his close collaborators or customs officials had received bribes for the waivers.
"The circumstances under which the waivers were recommended are such as to arouse the suspicion of any reasonable person," it said, adding it would continue investigations.
Rawlings switched Adam to trade and industry in March.
The commission, which held public hearings, said Owusu had been unable to account for 33 million cedis in excess income. It recommended that he be made to refund the money to the state.
Rawlings vowed to clean Ghana of corruption after seizing power for the first time in 1979.
He said last November when the inquiry was launched that it was designed to clear the air before this year's presidential and parliamentary polls.
Opposition newspapers have been saying Rawlings and his associates have been doing extremely well since he seized power for a second time in 1981 and restored democracy in 1992.
Obeng, leader of many trade promotion missions abroad, is widely seen as the prime minister Ghana does not have.
Newspapers alleged he had benefited from the sell-off of a state-owned enterprise and used front-men to conceal ownership of real estate, of companies and of a top Accra restaurant.
The report accused Adjei-Maafo, former presidential advisor in the key cocoa sector, of under-declaring his income from sources other than salary to the Internal Revenue Service.

It said he owned real estate, farms, a chocolate company and school. He bought one villa in the name of a son aged seven. "The commission finds the entire conduct of Dr Adjei-Maafo to be incompatible with holding such a high public office," it said.
Rawlings sacked Adjei-Maafo quietly in September when he scrapped the post of presidential advisor for cocoa affairs.
